title: Tax-credit developments: sales just before the application
question: Did the land or building behind a tax-credit development change hands in the three years before the application, what value did that sale set, and how does it sit against the acquisition cost in the application?
finding: Of 178 San Francisco tax-credit applications since 2007 that could be matched to a parcel, 53 show a sale date in the application year or the three years before, and the roll shows a value set by that sale for 37. The application’s land and acquisition line is on disk for 5 of those: in 3 the roll value is within a tenth of that line, and in 1 the value the sale set is less than half or more than twice that line (2550 Irving: $9,000,000 on the roll against $1,190,308 in the application, where the City bought the land itself for $9,600,000). Lot lines were changed within three years either side of the application in 62 developments.
how: Every San Francisco project in the State tax-credit list with an application year of 2007 or later, matched to parcels by address. A sale date counts if it falls in the application year or the three calendar years before; the list gives the year of the application, not its day. The value set is read from the rolls as in the purchase screens. Land and acquisition cost is the line of that name in the State committee’s staff report, which is on disk for applications from 2018. Lot changes come from the City’s parcel change log and parcel history.
limits: The roll records no price. The value that appears after a sale date is an indicator of the price, because California law re-sets assessed value to the price paid when a property changes hands; exemptions, a transfer of part of a property, transfers the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break that link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder would settle what was paid; neither is open data. In a purchase-and-repair deal the building is usually sold by the sponsor’s old partnership to its new one, at a price set by appraisal; in a new-construction deal the land is often leased from the City or a public agency and the acquisition line is small for that reason. Most of these buildings carry a welfare exemption, and a sale between related nonprofits may not re-set the value at all. The acquisition line can include buildings, legal and holding costs that the roll’s land-and-improvement value does not, and the site in the application can cover more or fewer lots than were matched here.
